For runners, that's a great way to end up injured.

The good thing about running is that only rarely do injuries happen suddenly (without gradually increasing pain & warning signs).

So you try to run a little farther, or faster in the same distance. If that over-stresses your body (eg, shin splints), do something else. Run your usual route then hit the elliptical afterwards.

Or spend more time stretching than last time. Or designate a non-running day (weights) each week, then next week, try to beat your last lifting/non-running workout.

You can ALWAYS do SOMETHING better. And you can always find something you can do that doesn't increase chance of injury. Further than that, "stop pushing if you're injured" is sort of in the 'no shit' category.

[Oct 2016]

In order to supplement the strategic positions of China's artificial islands, the PRC has announced that it will move forward with developing modular [VLFS](http://www.businessinsider.com/china-to-build-giant-floating-islands-2015-8) 'floating islands'. These platforms—the largest being roughly 3.2km long—will snap together "like legos" to form mobile piers, airports, hospitals, and military bases tourist attractions, allowing a high degree of strategic flexibility for the People's Liberation Army Navy.

Displacing 1.5 million tons, the VLFS will out-mass supercarriers by an order of magnitude, and their modular design will make them very resistant to sinking.

Aircraft carriers are traditionally limited in the number and types of aircraft they can carry, because any planes taking off from a carrier must have plentiful thrust to achieve take-off on a limited runway (and even then they must usually make use of a [catapult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_catapult), as well as have the carrier turn towards the wind). A VLFS configured as runway could accommodate aircraft that are larger, heavier, and slower than those that can be used on most carriers.

The VLFS is expected to have a top speed of 18 km/h.

Construction has commenced in Caofeidian, near Beijing. The project is estimated to cost 3.7 billion yuan (570 million USD).

###### Meta note since this isn't something China would include in any announcements: China has struggled to produce a traditional aircraft carrier in the past because Chinese engine designs are not powerful enough to achieve consistently safe launches. Our only actual carrier at the moment was bought from the Soviets, and it is rife with problems such as the steam-powered catapult losing steam. But IIRC we have stolen the designs of the US's newer electromagnetic catapult; so we've got that going for us; which is nice.
